Furthermore, the only system in the original 10 early deployment sites with a significant history of operations—the Rivium District ParkShuttle—operates primarily on a segregated transitway. To safely navigate the increased complexity of a dense multimodal environment in mixed traffic, technology developers have used several tactics to maintain safety: • Limiting AV operations to dedicated lanes • Operating AVs at lower speeds even in mixed-traffic conditions • Retaining safety attendants to provide human operation through the “tough spots” and to serve as an authority presence among passengers sharing a vehicle • Designing in the ability for remote monitoring of the fleet operations so operators can communicate and interact with a vehicle from an operations center when needed • Augmenting vehicle sensors with infrastructure capabilities and communications referred to herein as intelligent roadway infrastructure (IRI). Examples of these tactics are evident in the 10 early-stage deployments that have been tracked, and these tactics continue to be used in ongoing deployments. Phase II research concluded that to provide safety for all travelers in the AMD—and to assist AV fleets in complex intersection environments and to provide fail-safe redundant operational control—IRI can be a critical complementary element for large-scale deployments. With respect to increasing the safety of advanced technology AVs, the integration of IRI technology into the overall fleet operational control system through SAE’s cooperative driving automation principles (SAE International 2021b) may help the individual fleet AVs safely maintain their operating speed as they approach a complex intersection. A common observation from the pilot AV deployments is that any slowing of fleet AVs below the speed of the other vehicles in the traffic stream will increase the risk of human-operated vehicles colliding with the AV from the rear. IRI is also pursued for safety and coordination of normal roadway traffic and vulnerable roadway users, as exhibited by the U.S. Department of Transportation’s emphasis on roadway digital infrastructure to increase safety and reduce congestion (independent of AV deployment). A dense development setting is important for an AMD. A district with a significantly large number of origin-destination trips is necessary to justify the investment in AV fleets for public mobility and to provide appropriate return on investment for their deployment. Automation can be applied in various environments; however, a dense development district in which efficient access is lacking from traditional movement technologies because of congestion, low speeds, and parking issues is ripe for innovation. A vast majority of the 10 early deployment sites were of this nature. 2.
